runs.question: How does the NIST Generative AI Profile describe data privacy risks?

answer.text:
The NIST Generative AI Profile (NIST AI 600-1) treats data privacy as one of its twelve GAI-specific risks, in section 2.4 on pages 11 and 12. I could not use the search tool, which failed, so I read those pages directly.

**Main concern.** The profile says GAI systems raise several privacy risks. Its core worry is that training on personal data conflicts with established privacy principles. GAI system training requires large volumes of data, which in some cases may include personal data. The use of personal data for GAI training raises risks to widely accepted privacy principles, including to transparency, individual participation (including consent), and purpose speciﬁcation.

**Limited transparency about data sources.** Most model developers do not disclose speciﬁc data sources on which models were trained, limiting user awareness of whether personally identiﬁably information (PII) was trained on and, if so, how it was collected.

**Memorization and leakage.** The profile cites adversarial attacks that have pulled training data out of LLMs. During adversarial attacks, LLMs have revealed sensitive information (from the public domain) that was included in their training data. It also notes that this memorization may affect even rarely seen data.

**Inference of sensitive information.** Models may also produce details that were never in their training data. GAI models may be able to correctly infer P II or sensitive data that was not in their training data nor disclosed by the user by stitching together information from disparate sources. The profile adds that such inferences can harm people even when they are wrong. These inferences can have negative impact on an individual even if the inferences are not accurate (e.g., confabulations), and especially if they reveal information that the individual considers sensitive or that is used to disadvantage or harm them.

**Downstream harms.** Wrong or inappropriate inferences about PII can lead to further damage. The profile gives the example that predictive inferences made by GAI models based on PII or protected attributes can contribute to adverse decisions, leading to representational or allocative harms to individuals or groups.

The profile also links privacy to other risks. Its discussion of content safety notes that output restrictions relate to Data Privacy, among other risks (page 11). It also lists "Privacy Enhanced" among the trustworthy AI characteristics it draws on (page 12). I did not find suggested actions for privacy in the pages I read, so this summary covers the risk description only.

These inferences can have negative impact on an individual even if the inferences are not accurate (e.g., confabulations), and especially if they reveal information that the individual considers sensitive or that is used to disadvantage or harm them.
**Downstream harms.** Wrong or inappropriate inferences about PII can lead to further damage. The profile gives the example that
predictive inferences made by GAI models based on PII or protected attributes can contribute to adverse decisions, leading to representational or allocative harms to individuals or groups

.

The profile also links privacy to other risks. Its discussion of content safety notes that output restrictions relate to Data Privacy, among other risks (page 11). It also lists "Privacy Enhanced" among the trustworthy AI characteristics it draws on (page 12). I did not find suggested actions for privacy in the pages I read, so this summary covers the risk description only.
